title: Vortex-mediated spin current injection into two-dimensional superconductor NbSe2
authors: Meng Yang, Xiaolong Yin, Jingjing Liu, Yifeng Chen, Qinwu Gao, Hongxing Zhu, Danni Huang, Lang Chen, Shuo-Ying Yang, Junxue Li
abstract: Injection of pure spin current into superconductors remains a major challenge in superconducting spintronics. Previous studies have primarily focused on spin-polarized quasiparticles and spin-triplet supercurrents, while vortices, ubiquitous topological defects in type-2 superconductors, have been theoretically proposed as alternative carriers of spin angular momentum, yet direct experimental evidence is still lacking. Here, we report the vortex-mediated spin current injection in NbSe2/LiAl2Fe3O8(LAFO) bilayer, an Ising superconductor/ferrimagnetic insulator heterostructure. Under an out-of-plane temperature gradient and an in-plane magnetic field, the NbSe2/LAFO bilayer shows a pronounced thermoelectric peak near the upper critical magnetic field, which has the opposite sign to the conventional vortex Nernst signal observed in a single-layer NbSe2. The sign reversal suggests that the vortex flow induced by spin current injection is opposite to the flow driven by the temperature gradient, which is consistent with theoretical mechanisms including spin-vorticity transmutation and the inverse vortex spin Hall effect. By mapping the field temperature phase diagram, we reveal that the spin current injection occurs exclusively in the vortex liquid phase of NbSe2. Absence of the thermoelectric signal above the superconducting transition temperature further rules out the quasiparticle contribution. Our results establish vortices as efficient carriers of spin information in superconductors, opening a new route towards vortex-mediated superconducting spintronic devices.
summary: This paper investigates the injection of pure spin current into a superconductor using a $	ext{NbSe}_2/	ext{LAFO}$ heterostructure. By measuring a sign-reversed thermoelectric signal, the authors demonstrate that topological vortices act as efficient carriers of spin angular momentum. This opens a new pathway for designing vortex-mediated superconducting spintronic devices.
main_problem: Injecting pure spin current into superconductors remains a major challenge in superconducting spintronics.
main_result: The study reports a pronounced, sign-reversed thermoelectric peak in a superconductor/ferrimagnetic insulator bilayer, establishing vortices as efficient carriers of spin information.
method: Thermoelectric transport measurements were performed on a $	ext{NbSe}_2/	ext{LAFO}$ bilayer using an out-of-plane temperature gradient and sweeping an in-plane magnetic field.
model_or_system: The system is an $	ext{NbSe}_2/	ext{LiAl}_2	ext{Fe}_3	ext{O}_8$ ($	ext{LAFO}$) bilayer, an Ising superconductor/ferrimagnetic insulator heterostructure, studied in the vortex liquid phase of a type-II superconductor.
key_observables: Thermoelectric peak ($	ext{V}_{2\omega}$), resistance ($	ext{R}$), and the comparison of the signal sign relative to the conventional vortex Nernst effect.
important_parameters: Out-of-plane temperature gradient, in-plane magnetic field, and the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$).
main_assumptions: The observed signal is attributed to vortex motion driven by spin current injection, which is confirmed by the signal vanishing above $T_c$ and the sign reversal relative to thermal effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the theoretical mechanisms (VNE vs. VMSC), device setups for $	ext{NbSe}_2/	ext{LAFO}$ and control samples, and the field/temperature phase diagram showing the vortex liquid regime.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the challenge of spin current injection, details the $	ext{SC}/	ext{FMI}$ setup, presents measurements showing a sign-reversed thermoelectric peak, and concludes by confirming the vortex-mediated mechanism and its implications for spintronics.
why_interesting: The work bridges superconducting physics with spintronics by proposing a novel, measurable mechanism (vortex-mediated spin current) that can be probed using established superconducting transport measurements.
